clue.text: Appliances to cook with propane, possibly

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., the heavy range cookers
second meaning, read as two words: propane is an example of a gas, 'a gas'

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer into A GAS; 'possibly' warns that propane is just one instance. An Aga is a heavy British range cooker.
explanation.definitionFit: Agas are big cast-iron range cookers, a familiar trademark name for kitchen stoves in Britain.

clue.text: Gold on the rise in fashionable club

indicators.note: in places the reversed gold inside the fashionable word

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in 'the in thing'

indicators.note: in a down clue, on the rise means the gold word is written upwards, i.e. reversed

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Gold's value climbing inside a trendy nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'club' is a nightclub, but the definition means a golf club. 'on the rise' makes OR into RO, which goes 'in' IN.
explanation.definitionFit: An iron is a type of golf club with a flat angled metal head, used for shorter shots.

clue.text: Issue in item after item

indicators.note: read as 'the it in item goes after': the first two letters of the word item move behind the other two

explanation.surface: Something keeps coming up, one item after another.
explanation.walkthrough: The word IT sits at the front of ITEM; 'in item after item' says to put that IT after the rest of item, so EM comes first and IT follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue something, such as a sound or a statement, is to send it out or give it off.

clue.text: As discussed, hold what a setter needs to take the next steps?

definitions.text: what a setter needs to take the next steps

indicators.note: Something taken as discussed is taken as it is said aloud, so the sound of the word matters and the spelling does not.

parts.note: to hold something is to pause it, and that word spoken aloud gives these letters

explanation.surface: A crossword setter told to wait before working out the next stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is the gun dog, not the person who wrote the puzzle, and the next steps are taken on four feet. A hold in a countdown is a pause.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter is a breed of dog, and a dog's feet are its paws, so the answer is what it walks on.

clue.text: Naysayer checked up

indicators.note: Up in a down entry means the letters are to be read from the foot of the grid upwards.

parts.note: a horse that is reined is checked, and those six letters run upwards

explanation.surface: A background check being run on the man who keeps saying no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Checked up' looks like one phrase and is two separate instructions: a word for checked, then the direction to read it in. Reining a horse is holding it back.
explanation.definitionFit: A denier is someone who denies a thing outright — a climate denier, a Holocaust denier — which is what a naysayer does.

clue.text: Both hands cradling mellow brew

indicators.note: To cradle something is to hold it in your arms, so the word that follows is held between the letters just named.

parts.note: L and R are the abbreviations for left and right
to mellow is to age, which is what time does to wine and to temper

explanation.surface: Someone carrying a drink carefully in both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mellow' is the verb here, not the adjective describing the drink. Left and right stay at opposite ends of the entry, which is what makes the container so easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Lager is the pale, bottom-fermented beer that fills most British bars, and beer is brewed, so 'brew' is the drink it is one of.

clue.text: Kept going wildly in love with diamonds

indicators.note: Anything done wildly is done without order, so the letters beside it will not be found in the order printed.

parts.note: six letters of fodder
D is diamonds on a bridge scorecard, joined to the fodder

explanation.surface: A couple besotted with each other and with expensive jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kept going' is the survival sense — carried on existing — rather than the sense of continuing to move. Diamonds is the card suit, which is where its single letter comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: To live on is to carry on existing after something that might have finished you, which is what keeping going means.

clue.text: Great upset with a curtailed Mrs. Thatcher

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
with a means joined by an A, the letter added to the pool

indicators.note: the title loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Great upset as a certain Mrs Thatcher is cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mrs.' looks like part of the definition, but it is fodder, cut to MR.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret was the first name of Britain's first female Prime Minister, Mrs Thatcher.

clue.text: Tried again before satisfactorily taking part

indicators.note: Taking part of a thing is taking a piece of it and not the whole, so the letters wanted are a run inside the words given.

parts.note: the five letters wanted run across the gap between the two words, picking up the end of the first and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Somebody having another go before they manage to join in properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tried' is the examination sense of the verb — to sit a paper — which is why the past tense reads oddly on its own. In Britain a failed exam is resat the following year.
explanation.definitionFit: To resit an exam is to take it a second time after failing, so someone who resat it tried again.

clue.text: Birds keep moving south to the other side

indicators.text: moving south to the other side
indicators.note: south is the letter S, which moves from the front of the word across to the far end

parts.note: save means keep, as in save it for later

explanation.surface: Birds keep migrating south to the far side of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the S of SAVE moves: from the front to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Aves is the scientific name of the biological class that contains all birds.

clue.text: Vivaldi wrote a lot of these, anything but priestly at the core

definitions.text: Vivaldi wrote a lot of these
definitions.note: The setter defines by pointing rather than naming: 'these' is whatever the composer put on the page in quantity, so the phrase identifies the answer instead of standing in for it as a synonym would.

parts.note: anything but true means not true, so the phrase comes down to the one word

indicators.note: The core of a word is the middle of it, so only the letters at its very centre are taken.

parts.note: the two letters at the centre of the eight-letter word

explanation.surface: Vivaldi being described as anything but priestly.
explanation.walkthrough: Vivaldi was an ordained priest, known as the Red Priest for his hair, which is what gives the insult in the surface its sting. What a composer writes a lot of is notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Notes are the individual sounds a composer sets down on the stave, and a composer as prolific as Vivaldi produced them by the thousand.

clue.text: Cut sunscreen after vacation? Irrational, looking back

indicators.note: after vacation means the word is emptied of its inside, leaving only its outermost letters

parts.note: first and last letters, S and N

indicators.note: looking back means the irrational piece is read backwards

parts.note: pi is the best-known irrational number

explanation.surface: Someone trims a sunscreen tube after a holiday, acting on an irrational whim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vacation' plays on the holiday sense; here it empties sunscreen to SN. 'looking back' turns PI to IP.
explanation.definitionFit: A snip is a small cut made with scissors, as when snipping a thread.

clue.text: Case of doctor holding 50% of ribose for pharmacist?

definitions.note: A doser is anyone who gives out doses rather than a qualified chemist, and the question mark is the setter admitting that the job named is only roughly what the word means.

indicators.note: The case of a thing is the shell round the outside of it, so only the first and last letters are kept.
Half a word is half its letters, and here it is the back half that is used.
Whatever holds something keeps it inside, so the letters named next go within the letters before them.

parts.note: the outside letters of the word, its case
the back three letters of the six-letter sugar

explanation.surface: A doctor's bag with half a sugar sample in it, meant for the chemist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case of' looks like the bag the doctor is carrying and is in fact the instruction to keep only the outside letters. Ribose is the sugar that gives RNA its R.
explanation.definitionFit: A doser is one who measures medicine out in doses, which is the pharmacist's job seen from the patient's side of the counter.

clue.text: Solver occasionally recording loss of consciousness

indicators.note: Occasionally means every so often rather than throughout, so only every other letter of the word is taken.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of the word
an EP is an extended-play record, longer than a single and shorter than an album

explanation.surface: A crossword solver noting down each time they nod off over the grid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loss of consciousness' sounds like something a doctor would write down and means nothing more alarming than a night in bed. The EP turns up constantly in wordplay and is worth learning on sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleep is the ordinary nightly state in which awareness switches off, so the medical-sounding phrase describes it exactly.

clue.text: Ran into road gripping hammer, naked

indicators.note: gripping means holding, so the road abbreviation wraps round the stripped hammer
naked means stripped of its covering, so the word loses its outside letters

parts.note: the word hammer, which once naked keeps only its inner letters

explanation.surface: A runaway vehicle careers into a road where a naked man holds a hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naked' strips the H and R off HAMMER, leaving AMME, which RD grips.
explanation.definitionFit: To ram something is to run into it with force, so rammed means crashed into.

clue.text: Answer buried in rubbish, whichever way you look — every solution is something like this

definitions.text: every solution is something like this

indicators.note: buried in means placed inside, so the answer letter sits within the rubbish letters

parts.note: rot means rubbish; looked at both ways it reads ROT then TOR

explanation.surface: A puzzle answer lies hidden in junk, and you see the same thing however you turn it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buried in' puts A between rubbish read forwards then backwards, ROT and TOR. Every answer in this grid can be turned round to make another word, as AGAS gives SAGA.
explanation.definitionFit: Each answer here is a word that rotates into a new word when reversed, so each is a kind of rotator.

clue.text: Detector of speeding Lada cutting off learner in posh car

indicators.note: To cut something off is to lop it away, so the letter named goes from the word before it.

parts.note: RR is Rolls-Royce, the British byword for an expensive car

indicators.note: One thing put in another sits inside it, so these letters land between the two just named.

parts.note: the cheap Soviet-built saloon that was a standing joke on British roads
L is the plate a British learner driver must display, and it is the letter cut away

explanation.surface: A Lada cutting up a learner driver who is out in something expensive.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is in the cars: the cheapest saloon on the road barging past the dearest. Radar is short for radio detection and ranging, and is itself the same word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A radar gun is what the police point at passing traffic to measure its speed, so it is the detector of speeding.

clue.text: Perhaps watch author entering exhausted after striking editor

indicators.note: Something entering a word goes inside it, so these letters are planted in the middle of what follows.
To strike a thing out is to delete it, so the letters named come out of the word before them.

parts.note: someone exhausted is tired
ED is the masthead abbreviation for editor, and it is the pair struck out
the person writing the clue is its author, so 'author' is ME

explanation.surface: An exhausted author walking into the office having just thumped the editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking editor' reads as a journalist on the picket line and is an instruction to delete two letters. The author is the setter: ME is the crossword's oldest piece of self-reference.
explanation.definitionFit: A timer is any device that measures elapsed time, and a watch is one of them, which is what 'perhaps' is flagging.

clue.text: Advance payment desired when banks withdraw

indicators.note: when banks withdraw means the edges of the word are taken away, leaving the middle

parts.note: wanted means desired

explanation.surface: Money wanted up front, at a time when lenders are pulling out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' are the outer letters, W and D, not lenders; take them from WANTED.
explanation.definitionFit: An ante is a stake put into the pot before a poker hand is dealt, hence any up-front payment.

clue.text: How a service professional might address crazy mother missing daughter

definitions.text: How a service professional might address
definitions.note: The definition describes the word's use rather than standing in for it: madam is the form of address itself, and the woman being addressed is left unnamed.

parts.note: mad is crazy

indicators.note: What is missing has gone from the word, so the letter named is not written down.

parts.note: a dam is an animal's mother, the word a breeder uses
D is the genealogist's abbreviation for daughter, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A shop assistant coping with a furious mother who has turned up without her daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: The mother is the animal one, a foal's dam as printed in any stud book, which is why the human family of the surface leads nowhere. A waiter using the word is being polite, not stuffy.
explanation.definitionFit: Madam is the polite form of address a waiter, receptionist or shop assistant uses to a woman customer.

clue.text: See 14
Produced domestic broadcast

indicators.note: Something broadcast goes out in sound, so the word is to be heard rather than read.

parts.note: a domestic is a household servant, a maid, and that word said aloud gives these letters

explanation.surface: A home-produced radio programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Domestic' is the noun, not the adjective: the domestic was the servant who did the housework in a large British household. The two spellings are a standard homophone pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Something made has been produced — manufactured, put together, brought into being — so the two past tenses swap directly.

clue.text: Give up on eating small pudding

indicators.note: Whatever is eating something has it inside, so the letter named goes within the word before it.

parts.note: to desert somebody is to give up on them
S is the size on the label of a small shirt

explanation.surface: Deciding against even a small pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the pudding is the whole sweet course, whatever it turns out to be, not one particular dish. Desert and dessert are separated by the single letter the clue puts in.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage 'pudding' names the sweet course at the end of a meal, which is what a dessert is.

clue.text: Theatre agent returning after the opening of Amadeus to change the backdrop

indicators.note: after places the returning agent behind the opening letter

parts.note: rep is short for repertory theatre

indicators.note: the opening of picks the first letter of the word that follows

parts.note: its first letter, A

indicators.note: returning means the agent word is read backwards

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative, an agent

explanation.surface: A theatrical agent comes back after the first night of Amadeus to redo the scenery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' makes REP into PER, which comes 'after' A from 'the opening of Amadeus'. Amadeus is Peter Shaffer's play about Mozart, fitting the theatre picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To repaper is to hang new wallpaper, giving a room a fresh background.

clue.text: Let new enzyme at last inside cheese-maker's additive

indicators.note: the new and final letters go inside the rent word

parts.note: to let a property is to rent it out

indicators.note: at last picks the final letter of enzyme

explanation.surface: A new enzyme is finally allowed into the additives a cheesemaker uses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enzyme' looks like part of the definition, but only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Rennet is a curdling agent, traditionally from calves' stomachs, added to milk in cheesemaking.

clue.text: Offer to build, show and pay for house

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to put something forward
fourth meaning: to provide the money, as a backer puts up the funds
fifth meaning: to give someone a bed for the night

explanation.walkthrough: Five separate senses of one phrasal verb are strung together so the list reads like a builder's quote. The answer reads the same backwards, fitting the grid's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers proposing, erecting, displaying, funding and accommodating, each one a standard everyday sense of the same two words.

clue.text: Competition in pub ending in bad language and drama?

indicators.note: The ending of a word is its final letter, so that letter alone is taken from what follows.

parts.note: the last letter of the word
language and drama are both arts subjects on a school timetable

explanation.surface: A pub contest that finishes in swearing and theatrics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad language and drama' reads as one phrase about a row and splits neatly between the two halves of the wordplay. Darts is played on a board in the corner of most British pubs, in leagues that run all winter.
explanation.definitionFit: Darts is the pub game of throwing three darts at a numbered board, played competitively in bars across Britain.

clue.text: Discharge from nose not appropriate for anyone to see

indicators.note: 'Not' in front of a thing says it is absent, so the letter it names is left out of the word.

parts.note: a snout is a nose
U is the British film certificate given to anything the whole family may watch, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A nose in a state nobody should have to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the mildest of the British film certificates, printed on the poster of anything suitable for all ages. 'Not' looks like part of the description and is the instruction to delete.
explanation.definitionFit: Snot is the mucus that runs from the nose, which is a discharge in the plain medical sense of the word.

clue.text: Repositories for rubbish clues

definitions.meaning: the council dump on the edge of a British town, where household waste is taken by the carload
the hints and pointers that nudge somebody towards the thing they are after

explanation.surface: Bins for the crossword clues that did not work.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight through, the clue offers somewhere to throw bad puzzles away and the join between its two halves is invisible. A tip is the British word for the council rubbish dump.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip is the dump where household rubbish is taken, and tips are also the hints that point a solver towards an answer.

clue.text: Creed often ethical, but not entirely

indicators.note: Not entirely means the words give up only part of themselves, so the letters wanted are a run inside them.

parts.note: the five letters wanted run across the join between the two words, starting three letters into the first

explanation.surface: A set of beliefs that is mostly, though not completely, moral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely' qualifies the ethics in the surface and marks the hiding place in the wordplay, doing both jobs in the same three syllables. The word is the same read backwards, which is why it is in this grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a belief held as true — a creed is the doctrine professed, a tenet a principle within it — and they stand in for each other freely.

clue.text: Head over heels, finally passionate

indicators.note: In a down entry what goes over a thing sits above it, so these letters come first.

parts.note: nut is slang for the head, as in nutting somebody

indicators.note: Finally points at the end of the word, so only its last letter is used.

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Somebody falling head over heels at long last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head over heels' is one idiom in the surface and three separate instructions underneath. Being nuts about somebody is the very infatuation that idiom describes, which is why the definition sits so quietly at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To be nuts about something is to be wild about it, so 'passionate' is the same enthusiasm in politer words.

clue.text: Bucket brigade called out

indicators.note: Something called out is said aloud, so it is the sound of the word that counts and not its spelling.

parts.note: a brigade is a body of people working together, a team, and that word spoken aloud gives these letters

explanation.surface: A line of people passing buckets, summoned to a fire.
explanation.walkthrough: A bucket brigade is the chain of people handing water along to a fire, so the two words look inseparable and the clue prises them apart. Rain that teems is coming down hard — in Britain it is also said to bucket.
explanation.definitionFit: To bucket and to teem are both British for rain falling heavily and without let-up, as in 'it's teeming down'.

clue.text: Lascivious stare led reader without fear inside

indicators.note: Without a thing means it is not there, so the letters named are taken out.
Inside says where they were: the letters removed are the ones in the middle, not at either end.

parts.note: the two words run together, nine letters
dread is fear, and those five letters sit complete in the middle of them

explanation.surface: A reader taken through something frightening without turning a hair.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for fear is not hinted at by a synonym here — it has to be found whole inside two ordinary words, which is what makes the clue hard to see. A leer is the stare itself, not the person giving it.
explanation.definitionFit: A leer is a sidelong stare with unmistakable sexual intent, which is what 'lascivious stare' spells out.

clue.text: Set one plus one between 50 and 500

indicators.note: the two ones sit between the two numerals

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral 50
D is the Roman numeral 500

indicators.note: plus means added on, so the second one follows the first

parts.note: a means one
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A puzzle in arithmetic: one plus one placed between fifty and five hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: Laid and set both describe putting something down in position, as a table is laid or set.

clue.text: Stepped another way around old pothole?

definitions.note: 'Deep spot' is not the usual name for the thing; the setter is describing it instead, which is what the question mark is there to admit.

indicators.note: Another way around means not the way it is written, so the letters are to be set down in a different order.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder
O is the standard abbreviation for old, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: Walking round an old hole in the road rather than through it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stepped' reads as the definition of a clue about walking and is in fact the fodder. These eight letters turn round into TOP SPEED, which is the puzzle's theme doing its work.
explanation.definitionFit: A pothole is a hole worn deep into a road surface, so a deep spot in the tarmac describes one exactly.

clue.text: Poet, priest and where you can read about him

parts.note: Eli is the priest who brings up Samuel in the Books of Samuel

parts.words: where you can read about him
parts.note: the Old Testament, the part of the Bible his story is told in

explanation.surface: A poet, a priest, and the book the priest turns up in.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'him' at the end of the clue is the priest, not the poet, so the last phrase points back at Eli rather than forward to the answer. T. S. Eliot wrote The Waste Land and Four Quartets.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot is T. S. Eliot, author of The Waste Land, so 'poet' is the trade the surname is remembered for.
